title: Small business cry for cyber help
full_text:
It is too hard for small businesses to invest in cybersecurity and the government has taken away pathways, business groups say, as Jim Chalmers signals the government sees artificial intelligence as a key potential driver of productivity.
Treasury last week warned of only “measured” productivity gains and constraints across various sectors, but the Treasurer said AI would be the “first substantive and credible productivity growth accelerant in almost two decades”.
However, the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia and the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry have laid out significant challenges for small businesses to bulk up their cybersecurity as innovations in AI create both new challenges and opportunities for businesses.
ACCI said skills shortages were “constraining digital adoption, slowing investment in new technologies and limiting their ability to innovate” and that red tape and regulatory obligations were getting in the way of businesses putting time into cybersecurity and technology adoption.
COSBOA said small businesses were “significantly exposed” to AI threats – both from AI-enabled scams, and from inadvertently exposing private information on AI platforms, like sharing sensitive business or customer information.
It voiced particular concerns about the government’s decision to end the Cyber Wardens program that provided cybersecurity training for small businesses.
“The Cyber Wardens program, delivered by COSBOA with Telstra, CommBank and the Australian Cyber Security Centre, is the most trusted intervention to date in addressing small business cyber security training needs,” it said in a submission to a parliamentary inquiry on cybersecurity.
“The program has trained over 34,000 graduates since its inception and demonstrated measurable improvement in small business cyber behaviour.
“However, its commonwealth funding ended on July 31, 2026 with no current replacement proposed in the 2026-27 budget.
“COSBOA urges the committee to recommend renewed, ongoing investment in small business-specific training and guidance along these lines.” The Department of Home Affairs noted in its submission that under the government’s broader cybersecurity strategy, its CyberSmart Program would provide a certification framework for small and medium businesses.
ACCI said cybersecurity requirements for government procurement sometimes presented an “unnecessary barrier” for small businesses. “While robust cyber security requirements are justified where significant data, privacy or national security risks exist, imposing advanced certification or compliance requirements on low-risk suppliers may unnecessarily increase costs, administrative burden and barriers to entry,” it said. “SMEs already face a growing range of procurement-related compliance obligations … including ESG reporting requirements, modern slavery due diligence, workplace gender equality reporting, sustainability disclosures, ethical sourcing requirements, and various insurance obligations.”
